item.title: Early-Onset Dementia Symptoms to Look Out For
item.description:
There are few things more distressing than seeing cognitive decline in someone you love. It is even more difficult to accept when the loved one has not reached old age yet. Early-onset dementia has been known to affect people as young as 30. This means that by the time they reach their mid-60s, the age at which most neurodegenerative disorders begin affecting people, they are already in the advanced stages of decline.

As a loved one, early-onset dementia symptoms might catch you off guard, but if you can identify them early, you will be able to get the support you need. Early assessment often means that you can work with them to develop a plan for the rest of their lives and minimize some of the struggles they will have to face.

The Facts About Early-Onset Dementia

Early-onset dementia is not a disease, but a syndrome. This means that, unlike a disease which has a specific cause, early-onset dementia is merely a collection of symptoms that often do not have a singular cause.

In many cases, early-onset dementia is linked to Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, and frontotemporal dementia. It is currently estimated that cases of early-onset dementia in adults aged 30-64 have more than doubled in the United States in the last few years.

The fact that early-onset dementia is a syndrome, rather than a disease, means that it is difficult to define any risk factors. Studies suggest that genetics, environmental factors, and lifestyle are involved in the development of early-onset dementia.

Many neurodegenerative disorders are genetic, meaning if they exist in a person’s bloodline, there is a risk that they will be passed on from relative to relative. In the case of early-onset dementia, only a physician will be able to provide reliable data on its risk factors and likelihood of occurrence in your bloodline.

Early-Onset Dementia Symptoms

Early-onset dementia symptoms look almost identical to dementia in elderly people, except that they occur in young and middle-aged adults. Dementia of any kind is life-changing, but early-onset dementia affects a person’s family, career, and future.

They become dependent on loved ones at an age where they would otherwise be the provider or leader of their family. Their loved ones must be able to spot early-onset dementia symptoms early and obtain the necessary medical support they need.

Early-onset dementia affects a person’s memory, language and communication abilities, mood regulation, and daily functioning. This affects all the major areas of a person’s life, meaning that their lives will change entirely at some point. As alarming as it sounds, the fact is that they will become dependent on loved ones and medical assistance to function. It is crucial to notice the specific signs that your loved one experiences and intervene as quickly as possible.

Memory Loss That Disrupts Daily Life

If you have seen an elderly person go through cognitive decline, you will know what this looks like. It is repeated questions, frequently forgotten information that they recently learned, and an increased reliance on reminders. They might forget their favorite sports team, the route to work, or their own child’s name. While this can be alarming and hurtful, it is not intentional; they literally can’t help it.

Challenges In Planning or Problem-Solving

One of the areas of life that people struggle with most when it comes to dementia is in the area of finances. Their decreased ability to plan or problem-solve means that their bills accumulate, their salary goes untouched or is abused, and they often find themselves in debt. Besides finances, they might struggle with something as simple as following a recipe or conducting business online.

Difficulty Completing Familiar Tasks

When someone starts struggling with familiar or ordinary things, such as driving their daily route to work or going grocery shopping, it is a sign of cognitive decline. The inability to perform tasks as common and important as these means that they become dependent long before they ordinarily would. Without someone helping them, their quality of life will decline as fast as their cognitive abilities.

Confusion With Time and Place

Part of the daily functions that people with early-onset dementia symptoms struggle with is following time and knowing where they are and why. They might drive to the gym only to be panicked because they don’t know where they are or what they’re supposed to do there. Or they might start getting ready for work late on a Sunday night, hours before they are due at the office.

Trouble With Understanding Images and Spatial Relationships

One of the dangerous aspects of this kind of cognitive decline is struggling with depth perception and having balance that is thrown off. This makes tasks like driving incredibly difficult and dangerous because they cannot judge the speed or distance that other vehicles are traveling at. If your loved one is displaying this particular symptom of young dementia, it’s important to intervene as quickly as possible.

Problems With Speaking or Writing

Dementia affects different hemispheres of the brain, including the area responsible for communication. People with early-onset dementia symptoms regularly lose threads of conversations, have trouble joining in a new conversation, and often trail off because they have forgotten how to finish a thought. Not only does this affect their friendships and social life, but in many cases, it is disastrous for their career.

Misplacing Things and Struggling to Retrace Their Steps

It’s not unusual for a grandparent to misplace an important thing only to find it in an unlikely place. However, when it is your young loved one losing their phone and then finding it in the fridge, it is a different story. When they misplace items, they might start accusing others of having stolen them. They register the item’s disappearance, but can’t remember they were responsible for its last location.

Poor Judgment

When a previously grounded person begins making questionable and risky decisions, it is a sign that they are not thinking as they normally do. People with early-onset dementia usually begin acting out of character. This is most often first seen in their appearance, with grooming and hygiene that deteriorate quickly.

Withdrawal From Work or Social Activities

Part of the dramatic personality changes in someone displaying early-onset dementia symptoms is that they seclude themselves and drop off the social map. This is less noticeable in someone who was never sociable to begin with, but it is often a marked change in the extroverts. They may even decline visits from old friends, which often leads to isolation and depression.

Changes in Mood or Personality

Another clear indicator that someone is going through a major mental health event is that their moods become wildly dysregulated and, at times, their personality changes completely. A normally quiet and nurturing person might turn aggressive, or a naturally confident person might become shy and introverted. Though you might hope that it’s merely a phase, it might be an indicator of something more permanent and infinitely more worrying.

Hope For Their Future

Unfortunately, cognitive decline on this level is rarely curable. The best you can do for a loved one displaying early-onset dementia symptoms is to urge them to meet with a physician and get some tests done as quickly as possible.

You will likely have to help them with future appointments, timekeeping, note-taking, and medication. Another option is arranging support to perform these tasks. Other factors to consider include financial planning, their transportation needs, and potentially seeking legal advice if costly assets are involved in their estate.

Early-onset dementia is a life-changing thing to deal with. However, it is not the end of a person’s life, especially because they are still young. You might have to step up in a way you never prepared for, but you are never alone.

If you are supporting someone in cognitive decline, you also need support. Please consider meeting with a counselor for your own support. You can find one by visiting the online catalog of counselors or speaking with the reception team.

item.title: Intermittent Fasting and Eating Disorders: Can They Coexist?
item.description:
Intermittent fasting (IF) is all the rage at the moment. There are several types of IF, and people see results. But is there a danger in the practice of fasting, especially if you are diagnosed with an eating disorder? What about intermittent fasting if you typically engage in binge-eating behavior?

It’s important to first identify the three common eating disorders (ED) and then explain the pros and cons of intermittent fasting.

What is considered an eating disorder?

An eating disorder (ED) is not a diet someone has taken to the extreme. It is a mental condition that revolves around obsessive thoughts about food. It might be starving oneself to remain thin, purging food out of the system as quickly as possible, or eating tremendous quantities of food in a short time frame.

As many as nine percent of the American population will experience an eating disorder during their lifetime, according to the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders (ANAD). Eating disorders are among the deadliest mental conditions to date, with more than 10,200 people in the United States losing their lives from ED complications each year.

There are three common eating disorders: anorexia nervosa, bulimia, and binge-eating.

Anorexia Nervosa

Anorexia is the preoccupation with one’s appearance and the intake of food. Anorexic individuals may feel disgusted with their bodies or with food. They may attempt to starve themselves for control. Like with other eating disorders, choosing when and what to eat is a form of control. Some people use this to give themselves a sense of security when their lives feel out of control.

The person with anorexia will become a skeleton of their former self, weak, severely underweight, and unhealthy. Without enough nutrients, the body loses fat, muscle, and bone mass. Organ systems will eventually fail, and the heart will stop functioning. This behavior, if left untreated, is fatal. Not only from the inevitable shutdown of the body’s systems, but also the suicide rate for people with eating disorders is high, at around 26%.

Bulimia

While those with anorexia avoid food or eat very little, people with bulimia may consume food normally or in smaller amounts but obsess about ridding the body of the calories as soon as possible. These purging methods can include self-induced vomiting, laxatives, enemas, or extreme exercise. Just as dangerous as anorexia, bulimia destroys the digestive system, the esophagus, teeth, colon, and other systems from the constant purging behavior.

A bulimic may be at their average weight or underweight. With any eating disorder, mood and mental health are also affected. Depression, anxiety, and fear are prevalent. When the body lacks nutrients, the brain does not have enough fuel to operate, and thinking becomes cloudy. As with anorexia, if left untreated, bulimics may need intravenous feeding tubes and oxygen to save them from death.

Binge-eating

Binge-eaters indulge in behavior as if trying to fill a void in their life and in their hearts. A binge-eater may be overweight or obese. Although a binge-eater might plan the binge, they often consume large amounts of food mindlessly in a short period of time. They may eat late at night after their family goes to bed or stop on the way home at a fast-food place to eat hurriedly in their car and dispose of the evidence before they reach home.

While bingeing, the person may not feel the full sensation from their stomach as it stretches. Once the stomach begins to reach fullness in typical eating situations, the brain signals to slow down and stop eating. Food will lose its taste when the stomach is approaching its appropriate limit.

However, during a binge, those signals get lost. The binge-eater can consume thousands of calories and still not feel full. When the binge is over, the person will feel physically and emotionally sick and drained.

This behavior is also physically demanding, with extra fat stores, high blood pressure, high cholesterol levels, and heart attack or stroke risk. Depression, anxiety, guilt, and shame can weigh just as heavily.

What is intermittent fasting?

Intermittent fasting is a break from food to give the digestive system relief. The most common fasting practice is after dinner until breakfast (breakfast = break the fast). For some people, this could mean an eight-hour break. For others, it can mean twelve hours, depending on what time you finish dinner and if you do not have a snack before bed.

Studies show that intermittent fasting can greatly affect insulin resistance, blood sugar levels, cholesterol levels, blood pressure, and fat loss.

The most common intermittent fasting plans are 16:8, 20:4, 5:2, and alternate-day fasting.

With the 16:8 plan, the person fasts for 16 hours and eats meals in an eight-hour window. With the 20:4 plan, the fasting window is expanded to 20 hours, and the eating window shortens to four hours.

In the 5:2 plan, the person typically eats five days a week, then cuts back on the amount of food they consume two days a week (generally non-consecutive days). They might fast from food completely with only water or calorie-free drinks or limit their calorie count to a low number.

However, there are some drawbacks to intermittent fasting. Without regular food consumption, the blood sugar level can decrease, causing lightheadedness and moodiness. Many people begin to feel tired during the fast or extremely hungry, especially in the beginning as the change in eating shocks the body.

These are just a few of the IF plans that people use. But should you practice IF if you have been diagnosed with an eating disorder?

Should you practice IF if you have been diagnosed with an eating disorder?

Although intermittent fasting boasts impressive results both medically and with weight loss, practicing IF while dealing with an eating disorder can be devastating. People who suffer from anorexia nervosa need to learn to eat regularly. Depending on the severity of the mental condition, this lack of food (or controlling the fast window) can lead to a downward spiral.

Bulimics tend to fast intermittently, whether they realize it or not, as part of the purging process. They might eat a larger meal, then willfully starve themselves to purge or lessen the “damage” done by the food. The psychological aspect of controlling the timing and food portions is just as strong with IF as with bulimia. If you are diagnosed with bulimia, you should avoid intermittent fasting and speak with a therapist about a treatment plan.

Binge-eaters might be able to intermittently fast, but only under the supervision of a medical professional. It depends on the severity of the condition. Going long periods without eating will lead to a drop in blood sugar and increase irritability.

Some binge-eaters will actually binge once the fast ends. The binge raises the blood sugar (albeit probably much higher than is needed) and provides momentary happiness and relief. Unfortunately, this results in the binge-eater being caught in the vicious cycle again.

A medical professional specializing in nutrition and eating disorders can steer you in the right direction for a treatment plan, not only for your body but also for the mind. You should avoid fasting until you have been given the all-clear from your physician. It may derail your progress.

You should never engage in any extreme eating regimen until you have spoken to your physician and nutritionist. If you have been diagnosed with an eating disorder, consult your therapist. Intermittent fasting does have its benefits, but if it hinders your progress or robs you of your peace, then it is certainly not worth it.

If you do not already have a counselor, contact our offices today. We would love to help you and pray for you as you seek treatment and manage your relationship with food. Appointments are available with the therapists in our practice who have experience with eating disorders.

item.title: Breaking Birth Order Stereotypes
item.description:
In many families, certain roles quietly take shape as children grow up. These roles aren’t assigned on purpose, but they usually follow a pattern tied to what is called birth order. In this order, the oldest child is expected to be responsible and set an example; the middle children learn to adapt and stay in the background, while the youngest child is mostly seen as the fun one, or the eternal baby of the family.

These roles seem like harmless titles, but over time, studies have shown that they do influence what children think about themselves. They then shape confidence, personality, and even the kind of goals people set in life. Some people feel comfortable in the role tied to their birth order, although many others feel like they’re stuck and that it doesn’t match who they really are.

Letting go of these family labels is not something that is easy, but it is possible. The first step is to understand how birth order shapes our identity in the first place.

How Birth Order Affects Parenting

Parents don’t always mean to treat their children differently, but birth order mentalities seem to change parenting style sometimes. That’s because when the first child is born, parents are still new to everything, so they’re usually more cautious. They follow ‘the rules and recommendations’ of ‘good’ parenting.

They read parenting books, ask for advice, and pay closer attention to milestones. The first child grows up in this stricter environment, which begins to set the tone for them to identify with being more responsible.

a second or third child is born, things are usually a bit different. Parents already have some experience now, so they become more relaxed. Now with two kids, they are juggling more, and a tight order gives way to more chaos.

The middle child quickly learns to adjust to the parents, the older sibling, and then not long afterwards, maybe a younger one, too. By the time the youngest child enters a family that already has its routines, there’s less pressure, and parents have become more flexible and a bit more stable.

All of these differences form how each child sees themselves and their place in the family. The impact doesn’t end in childhood. It continues into adult life, guiding behavior and shaping self-esteem.

The Psychology Behind Birth Order

Psychologists have been studying birth order for years, trying to understand how it affects personality. One of the first to look at this closely was the Austro-Hungarian psychologist, Alfred Adler. He believed that birth order influences confidence, independence, and how people act in social situations.

Some studies suggest that firstborns are more likely to become leaders. They learn to take charge early and often try to meet high expectations. Middle children usually become good at building relationships because they spend time trying to fit in and stand out at the same time. Youngest siblings tend to be more relaxed but also work hard to prove themselves because they feel underestimated.

Birth order isn’t everything, but it matters

Birth order doesn’t exactly decide your future, although it has been proven to influence how you see yourself. It affects how you react to stress, how you form relationships, and how you handle goals and failure.

These patterns don’t apply to everyone, but they do influence how people approach challenges, relationships, and personal goals. Knowing more about these patterns helps us understand why we react a certain way in life. Understanding birth order is the first step toward building your own identity.

Firstborns Deal With

Firstborn children usually carry the weight of high expectations. Parents look to them to be the responsible ones. They are asked to help out more and are expected to always lead by example. This kind of pressure starts early and keeps building. For this reason, if you’re a firstborn child, you grow up feeling like you have to be perfect. Many first kids work really hard, feel like they have to take charge, and try to stay in control.

Sadly, this leads to stress and the feeling that they can never relax. Learning to take a step back and accept that it’s okay to also make mistakes can help firstborns feel more balanced and confident in who they are.

What Middle Children Go Through

Middle children face a different kind of pressure, since they aren’t the first, and they aren’t the last. They usually feel like they are just living in the background. Parents may not give them as much attention, and they may not have a clear role in the family.

To feel noticed, many middle children develop strong friendships outside the home, or they learn to adapt and find ways to be different. This builds independence, but can also lead to confusion about where they belong. As a middle child, you will feel stronger when you recognize your importance, ability to connect with others, and stay flexible in changing situations.

What the Youngest Children Struggle With

Youngest children are usually seen as both the easygoing and the spoiled ones. Since parents have relaxed a bit by the time the youngest comes along, they may give them a bit more freedom than they did with the other siblings. At the same time, this also means there are fewer expectations.

This freedom can be fun, but it also comes with downsides. In fact, most youngest children feel like they aren’t ever taken seriously. Even as adults, they’re still treated like the baby of the family, so they always feel the need to prove that they are capable, smart, and independent. As the youngest sibling in a family, you need to know that you grow stronger when you set your own goals and stop waiting for others to see your worth.

Ways to Break Birth Order Stereotypes

This is the way everyone gets strapped into a label they feel like they can never shake. Letting go of these ingrained roles in the family takes time and effort, but it’s worth the effort. You can start with some doable ways to break away from the labels that come with birth order.

Question family roles Ask yourself why you were always seen a certain way and if that role still fits who you are as you get older.

Focus on your strengths Make your own goals based on what you’re good at, not what your family expects from you.

Speak honestly Talk to your family about how you feel about the pressures tied to your birth order.

Try something new Stepping outside your comfort zone and routines helps you grow in ways your family might not expect.

Stop comparing yourself Your path and your success are your own, even if they look different from your siblings’ paths.

Create space for yourself Set boundaries when family expectations get too strong or limiting. Separate personal identity from family expectations.

Follow your passions Get more into hobbies and interests that truly reflect your personality, rather than what you just grew up being expected to like.

Build solid friendships Strengthen friendships with people outside the family to help you grow out of your set family role.

Be open to change Allow yourself to grow and change, even if change surprises others.

Let go of guilt You don’t need to carry the weight of an identity that was assigned to you. Accept that breaking free from that label is healthy and necessary.

Becoming the Person You Want to Be

Birth order plays a big role in shaping how you see yourself, but it shouldn’t define you. You don’t have to fit into a role just because it was handed to you early in life. When you understand how birth order affects your story, you gain the power to rewrite it.

By choosing your own path, you give yourself the freedom to become the person you really are, not just the role you were expected to play. Remember that so much of this role assignment is unintentional and subconscious. Many times, when we challenge it with our family, we can help them be free of these assigned roles, too,

Change is hard, especially when it comes to family. This process is easier said than done. Contact me today for help in growing more fully into your real self without restraint from birth order stereotypes.

item.title: Self-Care for Anxiety: Finding Peace in the Storm
item.description:
Have you ever found yourself in the middle of a turbulent situation? It might have been a literal storm or a challenging situation that made it nearly impossible to go about life as usual. One common challenge that many people face is anxiety. This is not only the everyday anxiety that affects us all, but crippling anxiety that makes it hard to function. Taking self-care for anxiety seriously is one way to cope well with anxiety in its many forms.

When you’re feeling anxious, it can feel like you’re in the middle of a storm, tossed about by racing thoughts, a pounding heart, carrying the feeling of dread, and a knot in your stomach. Anxiety is a common struggle, but it is one that’s often misunderstood and not attended to properly. Through effective support, you can bring your anxiety under control.

You’re not alone in your anxiety

Being anxious is a deeply human experience. We’ve all felt anxious at one point or another, and there’s a place for anxiety in our lives. Being anxious is a physiological response to danger, and that response can be lifesaving in certain circumstances. When you feel anxious about your first day at work or school, that isn’t necessarily a bad thing if it helps you prepare adequately. Anxiety can even help you as you do something simple like cross a busy street.

Many folks experience anxiety of the kind I’ve described above. It’s one of the many mechanisms in our bodies that allow us to navigate our world successfully. It is helpful to a point as it keeps you alert to your environment and enables you to prepare. However, anxiety can often become something more. Instead of being a help, anxiety can become a burden, keeping you up at night as your mind spins through worst-case scenarios.

This heavier and unhelpful form of anxiety is often referred to as an anxiety disorder. When anxiety no longer helps you, but instead burdens your existence, it is no longer doing what it was meant to. Anxiety disorders come in various forms, and many folks struggle with this more extreme form of anxiety. It can be triggered by anything from social situations, particular animals, or certain daily tasks, including sleeping.

Whatever your situation when it comes to anxiety and anxiety disorders, know that you aren’t alone. People from every background, faith tradition, or season of life face anxiety, and being anxious doesn’t necessarily mean that you’re broken or have weak faith. It is simply a challenging reality that you need support to deal with. One place to start is with intentional self-care.

What is self-care?

People matter, and one of the ways we show that people matter is by caring for their needs. You also matter, and self-care refers to the intentional practices and habits a person cultivates to sustain their mental, emotional, physical, and spiritual well-being. Taking care of yourself requires you to pay consistent attention to what you need so that you can flourish.

Self-care isn’t selfishness, though it’s always good to remember that even the best of the Lord’s gifts to us can be misused. If you’re inclined to ignore your own needs, a change in mindset is needed. Taking care of yourself is a form of faithful stewardship as you care for the mind, body, and life that the Lord has given you. Addressing your anxiety through self-care is a way not to retreat from life, but rather to prepare a way to return to it more fully.

What then is self-care for anxiety? Self-care won’t look the same for everyone, so if you aren’t a bath bomb and scented candle sort of person, that isn’t necessarily what you have to do. If you are, that’s great as a way to find rest and promote restoration. The main thing with self-care is to honestly appraise and understand your needs, then find healthy ways to meet those needs.

When dealing with anxiety, self-care can mean learning your own rhythms, being able to discern and listen to your body’s signals, and disrupting cycles of fear before they take root or escalate. Doing this and nurturing rhythms of life that help to ground you and create a sense of safety will help now and in the long term.

Self-Care for Anxiety – Daily Practices and Long-term Strategies

When anxiety is overwhelming, the temptation may be to try to do a major overhaul of your life so that you nip the anxiety in the bud and can get on with your life. This might seem like a good idea at first, but it can add to the sense of being overwhelmed, and often it isn’t sustainable. Rather, it’s important to have good follow-through on small daily choices, which can have a huge impact on your levels of anxiety over time.

In addition to these daily choices and practices, there are some longer-term strategies that can be implemented to help reduce anxiety and find ways to cope with it. The short and long-term tools work together to help you reduce the intensity and frequency of anxious episodes in your life. Some of the daily practices and long-term strategies for self-care include the following:

Daily Grounding In the morning, before you reach for your phone or iPad, spend five to ten minutes in quiet. Take deep breaths, name three to five things that you are grateful for, and offer up the day to the Lord in prayer.

Movement For many, their lives and work are mostly sedentary. Taking a walk during a work break or getting some exercise at the start and end of your day can help reduce anxiety levels and symptoms. Physical activity improves your mood and metabolizes stress hormones, helping you to calm your nervous system.

Better Sleep Poor sleep and anxiety feed each other. Better sleep hygiene helps anxiety. Try aiming for consistent sleep and wake times, avoiding screens before bed, and having a wind-down routine to help you sleep. These can all contribute to reduced anxiety and better emotional regulation.

Limit Media Consumption An anxious mind is more alert to and can absorb threats more readily. You can protect your mental well-being by setting boundaries around news and social media. Limit the amount of time you spend on media overall, avoid doomscrolling, and seek out balanced news coverage as well as media that also report on the good things happening in our world.

Regulate Your Breathing Anxiety often leads to shallow breathing and your body feeling like it’s in distress. Slowing and regulating your breathing helps to activate your parasympathetic nervous system, which signals safety to your mind and body. When you feel anxious, breathe in for four counts, hold your breath for four, then breathe out for six.

Journal Expressing your anxieties by writing them out helps to give them concrete shape. Externalizing them in this way helps give perspective and distance on those concerns, especially when you combine your journaling with prayer or meditating on a verse from Scripture.

Seek Community Being alone will often amplify your anxiety. Having meaningful and supportive relationships can be a great antidote to fear. The presence of trusted friends or a small group can be a bulwark against unwarranted fears. If you engage in regular conversation with someone like a spiritual director, they can help you pay attention to your inner life and how the Lord is present even in seasons of anxiety.

Sabbath Rest You need to give yourself room to rest, not just physically, but mentally, emotionally, and spiritually. Your weekly Sabbath practice could include stepping away fully from demands, screens, and productivity, and taking time to reflect on the Lord and His goodness. Humbly draw near to Him and seek His peace and rest (Philippians 4.4-7; Matthew 11.28-30).

Therapy Working with a trained and licensed Christian counselor is a useful long-term strategy to address anxiety. Your counselor will help you nurture greater emotional resilience and a deeper spiritual connection as you understand the roots of your anxiety. They can help you challenge the thought patterns that fuel your anxiety and work with you to develop tools to better cope with your anxiety.

This longer-term work won’t eliminate all challenges with anxiety from your life, but it can help you change your relationship with anxiety. Over time, you can become less reactive, more present and grounded, and more deeply rooted in the Lord’s peace that transcends all understanding (Philippians 4:7, NIV).

It is possible to bring anxiety, even the more intense forms of it, under better control. You don’t have to face the storm alone. With support, guidance, and compassionate care, you can begin the journey toward greater peace, healing, and wholeness.

If you’re ready to take the next step, I am here to help. Through counseling, you can explore the roots of anxiety, develop healthier coping tools, and discover a renewed sense of balance and hope. Reach out to my office today to begin your journey toward healing with Joseph Bennett.

item.title: Types of Relationships: Teen Dynamics
item.description:
If you’re a parent to a teen, you probably already know the importance of their relationships. They value friendships, sometimes even over family relationships. It’s not unusual for adolescents to spend enormous amounts of time with their peers and to value the opinions of their friends over anyone else.

Because of this hyperfocus on relationships, it’s important that you, as the loving parent you are, understand the types of relationships your child is in. It’s helpful to understand the unspoken rules and the teen dynamic of these relationships, too. Once you do, you can better determine the healthy and good relationships from the toxic and dangerous ones.

Below are some of the most common relationship dynamics your teen will face.

The Best Friend

A true best friend can be a beautiful gift from God. “A friend loves at all times” (Proverbs 17:17 NIV) isn’t just a poetic verse, but a truth and a benchmark for relationships.

A “best friend” is usually an obvious relationship in any teen’s life. They are mentioned often and are someone your child fiercely defends. And this can be a wonderful thing. When your child has a best friend, they have an advocate, a companion, and someone to hang out with both in and out of school.

Unfortunately, this best friend doesn’t always align with your values. When the best friend is the only voice that matters, the balance of power shifts. If your teens start to mirror everything about the friend, like their language, values, choices, and moods, it’s time to take a critical look at the relationship. Ask your teen some tough questions about morals, values, and behavior, and reestablish your own expectations and set boundaries.

The Frenemy

A frenemy is a “friend” who gives just enough effort for connection to keep your teen engaged but doesn’t necessarily have your child’s best interest at heart. You can spot these kinds of friends when compliments are peppered in sarcasm and when competition is more prevalent than support.

Your teen might feel confused by the contradictions in the relationship. You might too. They might remain loyal to their friend, even defending their action, but it might also shrink their confidence as they are forced to compete or defend themselves.

If you suspect your teen’s friend treats the relationship more as a competition or a battlefield than a friendship, it’s time to talk with your child. Show them that true friendship comes from love. And love shouldn’t leave them anxious or defensive.

The Opposite Gender Bestie

This relationship often starts harmless and platonic. It feels uncomplicated and even exciting, especially compared to the emotional intensity that comes along with dating. Your teen may feel understood by this person in a new and satisfying way.

This is because platonic friends of the opposite gender have a unique perspective on your life that a romantic partner or same sex friend just doesn’t see. Being in an opposite gender friendship can be as comfortable as it is exciting because there is no pressure to label anything, and you get all the benefits of dating without commitment to exclusivity.

These types of relationships are healthy, but they do require some strategy and planning. Emotional closeness without boundaries has a way of slowly shifting. Feelings can develop without a lot of obvious signs. Because the relationship already has emotional intimacy, the romantic bonds can hide behind it and habitual physical closeness.

To keep the dynamic healthy, encourage your teen to keep these friendships in group settings and maintain open conversations with you about where the friendship ends and where feelings begin.

The Habit

Some friendships exist more out of habit than deliberate choice. There’s something special about a relationship with longevity and history, but it’s also possible to outgrow a friendship. Maybe your child had a best friend in elementary school. Though the friendship is familiar, it no longer serves your child, and habit alone isn’t a solid foundation for any relationship.

Teens sometimes stay in relationships long after they’ve outgrown them because change can feel disloyal and off-putting. They might feel an obligation to remain connected even when the relationship no longer encourages growth or lacks other fundamental relationship elements.

As Ecclesiastes tells us, there’s a season for everything. That includes relationships. It’s important to help your teen understand that healthy relationships evolve naturally. Sometimes they grow and deepen, and other times, they fade away.

They may want to pull away from a friendship that doesn’t serve them, or they may have a friend pull away after years of friendship. In either case, they need to understand that this is a natural progression and not necessarily due to a relational misstep.

The Mission

Some teen relationships happen out of a desire to help the other person. Maybe your child sees another child who is sitting alone at lunch or who gets bullied on the bus. And they want to reach out to that child, encourage them, and be their advocate. These are relationships that originate in service and purpose and can be something you’re proud of as a parent. After all, God does call us to bear one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2 NIV).

While a relationship like this teaches empathy, compassion, humility, and patience, it can also have its challenges. Your teen might sacrifice their own needs or be negatively influenced by the one they are trying to help.

You don’t want to discourage them from helping others, but they need to balance their compassion with self-preservation. To properly serve others, your teen must not act out of guilt or obligation or even a desire for recognition, but with true godly intent.

The Hero

Every teen has someone they look up to. And a lot of times that person is in their friend circle. This person might hold characteristics that your child wishes they possessed. Maybe they are in a leadership role, appear mature or capable, or are successful in their social life.

Admiration itself can be good because it can inspire growth, motivation, and help your teen to set their own goals. But there is a fine line between inspiration and idolization. When admiration turns into idolatry, the relationship can turn from inspiring to toxic and sinful.

Remind your teen that no human should ever be their moral compass. Only God deserves that pedestal. Heroes can teach and inspire, but they cannot give your teen an identity or build their worth because that is found in Christ alone.

The Convenient

Some relationships are simply convenient. Maybe your child has a friend who is in the same classroom or bus route or enjoys the same type of after-school activity. These types of relationships are comfortable, low-maintenance, and that’s perfectly fine. In fact, these easy relationships are the gateway to more meaningful friendships.

The challenge comes when convenience supersedes your child’s discernment. Teens might stay in these easy relationships because it’s easier than thinking through their social choices or because getting out of them might feel awkward.

Help your teen reflect on these relationships. Is this convenient relationship one that they’d keep even if it became inconvenient? If it’s not, it’s important not to let them get too invested, but to enjoy the relationship for what it is, with no expectations. Is this relationship healthy for their spiritual life? If not, they need to prioritize their own growth rather than what is easy.

Teen Therapy

Sometimes teens need a safe space that isn’t home, and they need a listening ear that isn’t yours. They need someone who is trained to actively listen without judgment and who is trained to help them understand their own emotions, relationship dynamics, and the impact on their lives.

Therapy can help your teen learn more about their relationships and how to handle conflict, set boundaries, and recognize the signs that indicate a relationship isn’t serving their best interests.

Therapy isn’t just for your teens. Even rock star parents can feel overwhelmed during the tumultuous teen years. You’re dealing with emotional and hormonal shifts, new social pressures, identity questions, and spiritual growth, all in an intense seven-year period.

If your teen is struggling in their relationships, or you feel unequipped to handle their complex teen years, schedule a session with one of the counselors in our association. These professionals will walk beside you and your teen through all the confusing, stressful, and successful moments that make up the complicated and beautiful time called adolescence.

item.title: How Overlapping Stressors Affect Male Mental Health
item.description:
Many men carry the heavy burden of the expectation to handle everything at once. Work demands are piling up alongside family responsibilities and financial pressures, and male mental health often takes a backseat to these pressing issues.

The problem isn’t the stress that’s present; it’s the way that each area of stress is layered on top of one another, creating a burden that is increasingly difficult to carry. Alone, each of these may be manageable, but together they produce an overwhelming burden that seems unbearable.

Men have been conditioned to approach these situations in a certain way, which creates the challenges. It is an unspoken script of society that says men must manage multiple pressures simultaneously to be considered capable and strong. By admitting that the combined weight feels crushing, they feel as though they are admitting failure.

The reality is that overlapping stressors don’t just add up; they multiply. Relationship strain intensifies when paired with the stress of a demanding job. When health concerns emerge, financial worry deepens. Each area of life affects the others, creating a cycle that seems impossible to interrupt.

Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, NASB

When Work Stress Bleeds Into Everything Else

The line between professional life and personal life becomes increasingly blurred and creates implications for male mental health. Work stress doesn’t stay at work. It follows them through the door, shapes their interactions with the family, and influences their presence in other areas of life.

It’s impossible to feel fully present for a spouse or children when the mind is preoccupied with deadlines and thoughts of job insecurity. They find their minds tethered to unfinished tasks and unresolved problems.

A specific form of tension arises when men feel they are failing in multiple areas of life. They may struggle at work to maintain focus and productivity, and at home, they are emotionally distant and unable to engage with their family.

Christian counselors often see how this division of attention creates a guilt that stacks another form of stress onto the pile. This overlap of stressors suggests that there is no reprieve in sight. Counselors recognize that men feel that addressing one issue appears to neglect another. This results in a feeling of being trapped in a pattern that falls short of expectations for being a good father, husband, and coworker.

For I am confident of this very thing, that He who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus. – Philippians 1:6, NASB

The Hidden Toll of Financial Pressure

It doesn’t matter what area of life it is; money issues will always be present in the decisions. Financial stress isn’t limited to worrying about paying bills or saving for the future. It changes how someone moves throughout their day. It influences choices about what to eat, when to go out to see friends, and when to address health issues that may require spending money.

For many, financial responsibility is deeply tied to their identity and worth. This creates an economic strain that harms their mental well-being. This in turn creates anxiety, depression, or behavioral issues that affect everyday life and being present in the lives of their family.

When this stress overlaps with other pressures, the challenge becomes intensified, and men can face compounded anxiety. When men fear they cannot provide for their families, and that fear intersects with concerns about disappointing loved ones, they find it challenging to maintain stability and preserve dignity.

Christian counselors can easily identify these fears that often go unspoken because men do not want to admit to financial struggle and feel inadequate on top of all the stress they are already struggling with.

This silence about financial problems leads to isolation and prevents men from seeking help. Combined with relationship difficulties or health concerns, there is another level of being overwhelmed that begins to feel paralyzing.

And my God will supply all your needs according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:19, NASB

Physical Health Problems That Compound Mental Strain

Mental well-being and physical health are reciprocally related. When health issues emerge with other stressors, the impact on the mental health of men can significantly intensify. Chronic pain, illness, or declining physical capability doesn’t hide in the shadows.

It affects a man’s ability to work, engage with his family, and maintain a marriage in ways that previously provided him with joy. This loss of physical capability raises questions about identity and the future, as men have allowed it to shape how they are defined.

Health concerns compound existing pressures in complex ways. A man who deals with a chronic condition while managing work stress and family responsibilities must decide how to allocate limited energy. Every activity he engages in will require calculating the physical cost. This consideration adds another layer of complexity to the stressors they face that others may not recognize.

Therefore we do not lose heart, but though our outer man is decaying, yet our inner man is being renewed day by day. – 2 Corinthians 4:16, NASB

Relationship Dynamics Under Pressure

Men facing multiple stressors often see the strain in their relationships. Spouses may notice withdrawal, irritability, or emotional distance before the man recognizes how overwhelmed he has become.

The competing demands of work and finances, along with other pressures, leave little energy for emotional availability for marriage and home life. The result is a painful paradox in which connection and support are needed, but less accessible.

Relationship problems arise from and contribute to other stressors, making it difficult to address one without the other. Struggles at work, combined with a short temper at home, lead to conflict, which is another source of stress.

Financial pressure at home and related relationship strain give rise to economic worry. Health issues that limit intimacy or shared activities create distance between partners. It is a vicious cycle in which one stressor affects another.

Christian counselors observe that this means they underestimate how much these relational rifts compound their overall stress. When emotional support is most needed, its absence makes every other burden heavier.

Addressing the dynamics of the relationship is essential not for the relationship itself, but to create the foundation necessary to address different challenges. It is helpful for men to acknowledge their vulnerabilities with their partners, thereby creating opportunities for shared problem-solving rather than an isolated struggle.

Be devoted to one another in brotherly love; give preference to one another in honor. – Romans 12:10, NASB

Moving Toward Wholeness and Support

With recognition that overlapping stressors require different approaches, there is a path forward to overcome these challenges. Trying to power through the significant pressures simultaneously often leads to a breakdown rather than a breakthrough.

Men who acknowledge that seeking help isn’t a weakness find wisdom as they use practical responses to complex circumstances. Faith is one way to develop a framework for understanding human limitations and dependence on God, and community reflects strength rather than failure.

Moving forward means making choices that may feel counterintuitive. Setting boundaries at work, being honest about one’s emotional capacity, and asking for help with responsibilities may seem illogical when it comes to reducing stressors. But recognizing that mental health isn’t separate from practical circumstances is a small step toward managing one area of stress at a time.

As one area of stress is managed, breathing room enables the management of other pressures. Moving forward doesn’t mean perfection or the elimination of all stress. It involves developing a sustainable way of navigating difficult situations and maintaining connection with oneself, others, and God. This is an acknowledgment of the reality of male mental health challenges and the possibility of finding support and renewed strength for the journey ahead.

Bear one another’s burdens, and thereby fulfill the law of Christ. – Galatians 6:2, NASB

item.title: Social Anxiety: One of the Primary Causes That People Overlook
item.description:
If you dislike crowds, avoid small gatherings in general, or if the mere idea of being perceived by others makes you nervous, there’s a good chance that you have social anxiety. Social anxiety causes you to feel vulnerable when you are around others because you feel open to being evaluated, criticized, or judged by them.

You don’t have to be performing in public on stage; almost every interaction or conversation makes you feel unsafe, as if all of your words and actions are being scrutinized or judged.

Social anxiety causes you to miss out on much of life. Until you begin to understand why you feel anxious around others, and that you can deal with that anxiety once and for all, you might spend the rest of your life avoiding social situations and withdrawing from people.

Your need for space and time alone to recharge is valid and helpful, but your fear of other people’s judgment is unhelpful and will hold you back in life. You have got what it takes to uncover the truth behind social anxiety, face it, and deal with it once and for all.

Social Anxiety Causes You May Have Overlooked

Some people grow up being constantly criticized by a parent. It takes decades to realize that the comments they make, which are offered in the form of advice or concern, are little more than thinly veiled insults or statements that only cause you to feel ashamed of yourself.

“You don’t look good in that color,” or “It’s time you went on a diet,” might sound bluntly honest, but over time, statements like these simply make you self-conscious. Even when these statements are sandwiched between compliments, they don’t boost your self-esteem; quite the opposite.

Sometimes it is your oldest friends who hurt you the most, even without meaning to. Some old jokes go on too long, especially when you or your mistakes are the punchline. It is hard to stand up for yourself to family or friends, because you always run the risk of looking as if you can’t take a joke or that you’re overly sensitive.

The same goes for teachers, employers, romantic partners, or colleagues who belittle you or criticize your efforts. While some criticism is valid and helpful, constant microaggressions or subtly antagonistic statements erode your self-worth over time and cause you to have serious self-doubts.

When you peel back the layers of social anxiety, you will find shame, guilt, and fear. You will also find an inner critic, a voice that agrees with other people’s negative statements and echoes them. “You’re inadequate, no one likes you, you failed, just as expected.” You have likely been repeating these kinds of statements to yourself about yourself, reinforcing a toxic narrative that destroys your confidence and leads to more shame and embarrassment.

Social anxiety, at its most basic, is your nervous system stuck in a self-protective freeze mode. A gathering of people might look like a threat because there is a risk that you will look foolish in some way.

You might be a parent in your mid-30s participating in a school event, all the while feeling like a child facing down school bullies in the form of other parents. Even if nothing negative happens, you might still end up replaying events in your mind, finding the moments when you said or did something you regretted, or berating yourself for not doing or saying certain things. Even when people don’t hurt you, you find a way to hurt yourself because you feel as if that’s what you deserve.

Facing Your Opponents

Beneath social anxiety, there is often a cocktail of low self-esteem, shame, guilt, and fear. To avoid feeling these things, you have learned to avoid people, probably because of some past experiences that led to you feeling inferior or insecure.

You will never properly overcome social anxiety by avoiding people. Instead, you must confront your two biggest opponents and correct the narrative about you. The first opponent you must face is your own inner critic; the second is your outer critic or bully.

You begin to break the shame cycle by being self-reflective. Begin taking note of the way you speak to yourself, particularly when you feel as if you have failed or when you regret something. What do you tell yourself? Are there any names you call yourself, and if so, where do they come from? Social anxiety causes people to be withdrawn but not necessarily self-reflective; it takes effort to refrain from bullying yourself.

As you begin to practice self-compassion, you will find the strength to confront your outer critics. This can be hard, especially if they are family members, friends, or loved ones. Some of the people who have bullied you the longest are also the ones who know you the best, which makes their words cut deeper.

It’s not easy to tell a parent or sibling that you’re sick of the way they pick on you, or to tell a close friend that you feel as if they always disrespect you and don’t give you enough credit. When you can confront these people, though, you will have conquered a large chunk of shame that has been holding you back.

If you can’t find the words to confront your bullies, start by writing them down in a journal. Write down the specific things they have said to you so that you can quote them back accurately. Also, write down any emotion you can name that their words have made you feel.

People may have hidden their insults within compliments, or framed harsh criticism as humor, but your emotions can’t be gaslit. You know where it hurts. You can’t heal these wounds by avoiding situations. You must turn and face the things you have been running from.

Feeling Seen, Feeling Safe

Perhaps you have experienced the intimacy of having someone truly see you, understand you, and affirm you before. It can be a deeply uncomfortable and even triggering experience. Not everyone is out to get you, though. There are kind souls in the world, people who have also been hurt and have learned to be gentle with their words. You miss out on meeting them when you allow social anxiety to steer you away from others.

There is a story in the Bible of a blind man who sat huddled up in his cloak in the city square, waiting every day for people to help him with food or money. When Jesus passed by one day, the blind man yelled out desperately for Jesus to heal him of his blindness. Of course, Jesus had compassion on him and healed him, despite his followers trying to silence the man and keep him from Jesus.

It seemed like this man had accepted his lot in life, that he was content to remain what everyone else saw him as: a blind beggar, unworthy of help. When chance came, he flung off his old identity, begged for a new one, and got what he asked for.

Don’t let life and new opportunities pass you by. You are not stuck with your identity, and you don’t have to live up to others’ low expectations of you. You can see yourself in a new light and be seen and accepted by others who will love and value you. All you have to do is stand and be prepared to move from the familiar and comfortable situation you’ve been in.

If you have begun the work of healing social anxiety and shame, you likely need encouragement and support. We can connect you with a counselor who will walk alongside you as you continue to heal and break the shame cycle. Please contact our reception team for more information, or consult our online catalog to find a counselor today.

item.title: Mourning the Life You Once Had
item.description:
You look in the mirror, and all you see are the crow’s feet and gray hairs popping out of your eyebrows. You wake up, and the moments of chaos, messy fingerprints on the refrigerator door, and piles of laundry from your children are no longer there. You come home to an empty house now because someone left, even though you made a promise to one another.

Many people experience grief, but you might be surprised how many of the grief-stricken people you encounter are not grieving the loss of a close family member, friend, or even pet. They have lost a previous version of themselves or life that they long for.

Everything Changes

Life changes, and it takes with it our careers, our social status, and even our youthful bodies. Maybe you have been recently fired from a job you loved or one that you voluntarily left, hoping to pursue something bigger and better. Perhaps your friend group, the one that seemed so solid and united, has fractured over gossip or misunderstandings.

It could be that your once pristine complexion has become withered with wrinkles, as if it has morphed into a road map that could take you back to the life you once lived. Maybe it is that the person you thought you would spend the rest of your life with suddenly chooses to walk out. There are endless ways and reasons your life can change, and most of them are beyond your control.

No one has a funeral for their youth or wears black to mourn the loss of their best friend who moved to Cleveland. Still, it is perfectly normal to wake up one morning and mourn the life you once had.

It is easy to get caught up in the day-to-day hustle and bustle while juggling the weekly menu, heavy to-do list, and chauffeur duties. But what we fail to recognize in those moments when our inboxes are jammed full of requests, and our floors are covered in dust bunnies, is that these moments will pass. One day, you wake up to a life that you were not expecting nor prepared for, and now there is a mourning for some version of yourself that you have lost.

Some people think fondly about the moments when their knees did not crunch as they walked down the stairs. Others mourn the fact that they do not turn the heads of potential suitors the way they once did. Some people miss the chaos of child-raising and the constant influx of questions, messes left in the kitchen from an overnight teen raid, and the butterfly kisses before bed.

You might miss the satisfaction you got from accomplishing a complicated task at work or the praise you received when you made a large sale. Or maybe you just miss the younger version of yourself that still had so much to look forward to, with so many milestones unmet and potential paths to pursue.

The good news is that your story is not over. You may think that your best years and best experiences are a thing of the past, but as long as your heart is beating and there is air in your lungs, God is not through with you, no matter your age and stage in life. God has you alive, in this moment, for a purpose. You have a purpose.

Embracing the Present and the Future

Hearing the truth that God has a plan, still, even in this advanced stage of your life, is one thing, but overcoming your natural tendency to mourn the loss of your former life is another. You can know the truth and still not be able to control the natural emotions that you feel.

What should you do when you feel like your best years are behind you or that your former life was a lot more satisfying than your current one?

When you catch yourself longing for the past, remind yourself that nostalgia has a way of highlighting the good while blurring the struggles that came with it. Remember that road trip you took with your bestie when you got a flat tire, a bug in your salad, and the hard mattress in the cheap hotel? You may look back and laugh at the mishaps now, but in that moment, no one was laughing.

You may have seen this phenomenon happen after a death, too. Those left behind tend to glamorize their deceased loved one, choosing to dwell on the positive aspects of their life and glossing over the negatives. The same mental processing that allows you to do this is also tricking you into remembering a more glamorous version of your past, free of the bumps and dips of reality.

Every season of life carries both joy and difficulty. Just as you once found purpose and fulfillment in previous stages, you can find it again. You can do it now, right where you are.

One way to move forward is to practice gratitude. Instead of solely mourning what was, make it a deliberate habit to recognize what is still beautiful in your life. Maybe it is the wisdom you have gained, the friendships that have deepened, or the new opportunities that are just now unfolding. Or maybe it is just the fact that you have stumbled across these words, telling you that you are not alone and are loved.

Even in moments of loneliness or uncertainty, there is always something to cherish. God Himself came down to Earth to save your soul because He loves you. That alone can bring delight.

Another key to embracing the present is to lean into future growth and opportunities. What dreams have you set aside? What skills have you always wanted to learn? What relationships could you restore or nurture? Life may not look exactly the way it once did, but that does not mean it can not still be meaningful, vibrant, and full of God-given joy and God-directed purpose.

God does not change

While your life, your appearance, and your relationships may change, one thing that is consistent is God. God is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Just because your life may look different than it did one, ten, or fifteen years ago, does not mean that God has changed along with it.

God does not age, fail, or leave you. God is, and always will be, your constant companion. What a great relief to know that no matter what you go through, where you go, or how your circumstances change, the God who created the universe so many years ago is with you and loves you!

Your Identity in Christ

Most importantly, remember that your identity is not tied to a single season in your life. You are more than your youth, your career, or your role as a parent, spouse, or professional. You are continually becoming the God-appointed version of you. You are shaped by your experiences, strengthened by your challenges, and guided by the One who still has great and mighty plans for you. No wrinkle or unresolved past can change your true identity as a child of God.

Seeking Help

If you find yourself mourning the past, acknowledge it, but you do not have to stay there. If you need help walking through this stage in life, do not hesitate to seek help from a professional Christian therapist. Sometimes all you need is a gentle reminder to step forward in faith, knowing that the life ahead of you still holds purpose, beauty, and joy.

Connect with a therapist on this site to see how they can support you and help you find joy in this new season.

item.title: The Grief That Has No Funeral: Finding Peace After Pregnancy Loss
item.description:
It’s hard to know what to say after a pregnancy loss. And because we don’t know, we often stay quiet or say the wrong thing in hopes of offering some comfort. This grief gets folded up and tucked away because the world around us doesn’t quite understand where to place it.

We don’t have a gathering, and no announcement is sent out. People aren’t dropping by to offer meals and help around the house. Life keeps moving. There is no casserole brought to the door, no sympathy card in the mail, and no formally recognized time to step away from your daily life and mourn what was lost.

In the middle of this heartache, you’re left holding something hard to name. It could be an early pregnancy miscarriage, a stillbirth, or the loss of a baby shortly after delivery. The love you had for this baby is real, and so is the grief that accompanies the loss.

Women and families find themselves mourning in silence and pressed against a culture that tends to move on quickly. What seems like overreacting or being too sensitive is simply being a parent who lost a child, and that loss deserves a name.

The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, NIV

The grief of pregnancy loss is real, even without a name

One of the most heart-wrenching things about this kind of loss is the absence of language for it. There is no universally recognized title for parents who have lost a baby to a miscarriage or stillbirth, as there is with a spouse who loses a partner or a child who loses a parent. This absence of language creates a gap where grief can start to feel like something you’re not supposed to have.

Perinatal loss carries a deep grief that’s not determined by how far along a pregnancy was. There’s no question that emotional bonding begins the moment pregnancy is confirmed and sometimes long before. The excitement of planning for a child’s arrival is real.

But when it ends, grief will arrive with full weight as it does with any significant loss. It could be numbness, waves of unexpected crying, or a persistent emptiness that lingers daily. Some days feel manageable, and others, like a due date on a calendar or a baby shower invitation in the mail, can return everything to the surface without any warning.

Some Christian counselors specialize in this type of bereavement for parents. These counselors understand the complexity of this grief and how it is layered. This allows them to help parents move through this grief at their own pace.

Can a mother forget the baby at her breast and have no compassion on the child she has borne? Though she may forget, I will not forget you! – Isaiah 49:15, NIV

The Isolation That Can Follow a Silent Loss

When grief doesn’t have a public ceremony, people can feel alone. Friends and family are left unsure what to say, so they remain silent. Sometimes, coworkers are not informed of the pregnancy, resulting in a lack of acknowledgment of what was lost. It seems social media is inundated with announcements of healthy pregnancies and new babies, leaving you wondering where you belong.

The isolation that follows this loss is a natural response to grief that was never given room to breathe. Most of the time, it compounds over time, especially when a loss occurs more than once – the guilt and sense of spiritual abandonment that surfaces in isolation deserves to be witnessed. Holding grief on their own has a way of hardening and becoming a weight that shapes how you see yourself in your faith without even realizing it.

In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans. – Romans 8:26, NIV

How Faith Speaks Into the Pain of Pregnancy Loss

Christian women and families face spiritual wrestling with pregnancy loss. They question why it happened, whether their prayers were answered correctly, or if this is some punishment. These are legitimate questions, and they’re not a sign of weak faith. These questions reveal your heart, which is honest and engaged with its faith.

Scripture does not tell us to shy away from lament. We can read the book of Psalms for raw, unfiltered cries to God that don’t resolve quickly. This is our permission to take it all to God.

Faith isn’t asking us to process our grief in a tidy way. It simply suggests that we come as we are. That is not a small thing. In a world that expects us to manage, push forward, and perform, being welcomed into the presence of God without having it together first is an act of profound grace.

Many women find that, with the support of a Christian counselor, God is present in the loss. They begin to realize that God is never distant from the places that we hurt the most. He grieves with us, and the child that was lost was known by Him before the news of pregnancy became a reality. This carries a meaning that no cultural script can replicate.

Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart. – Jeremiah 1:5, NIV

Taking the First Steps Toward Healing

There is no easy or straight road to healing after a pregnancy loss. Unlike any other grief, there is no timeline and no comparison to someone else’s experience. The important aspect is that healing is possible, and you don’t have to find it alone.

Allowing yourself to grieve fully may look like creating a small memorial or writing a letter. Having a support group or others who understand the specific loss is one step toward healing.

It’s OK to permit yourself to feel something other than grief, such as joy or laughter, without interpreting that as a betrayal of the child you lost. Grief does not require permanence. It will shift, and as it does, allowing yourself to move with it rather than against it is part of what healing looks like.

Christian counselors are trying to help you identify what grief has done to your emotional health and your faith. They can walk you through rebuilding hope and faith without forgetting the loss. This allows you to make room for the loss in a life that continues to move forward.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, NIV

Finding Peace

Pregnancy loss rarely gets a ceremony, but it asks everything of the people who carry the weight of this grief. It requires endurance in the face of silence and faith in the face of unanswerable questions. It asks for resolve in the face of a world that does not fully understand what was lost.

You are not required to minimize it to make others more comfortable. There is no requirement to perform recovery before you are ready. There is a God who numbers the hair on your head, and He knows and loves the child that you carried. This is a love that does not require public acknowledgment to be legitimate, nor does it require a certain number of weeks to matter.

Your grief is valid, your loss is seen, and the road to healing was not meant for you to walk alone. There is support available if you take the first step to reach out. You can contact a member of our reception team to get connected with the counselor who has faith-based approaches that will help with pregnancy loss and grief.

He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away. – Revelation 21:4, NIV
