item.title: Hidden ADHD Symptoms in Adults
item.description:
So many adults are living with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and have no idea that this could be part of their struggles. This isn’t happening because ADHD symptoms are rare. It is because the symptoms do not look the way people expect. The hyperactive child bouncing off of classroom walls is the typical image that most people see when they think about ADHD.

However, in adults, the ADHD symptoms show up quietly and are often mislabeled as laziness, poor character, or anxiety. For adults who have spent years wondering why life seems harder than it should be, recognizing what ADHD actually looks like becomes life-changing.

Why ADHD Symptoms in Adults Look Different

The hyperactivity that defines ADHD in children shifts inward as people grow older. Adults tend to experience constant internal restlessness or a mental hum that never quite settles. Sitting through a meeting and trying to follow a conversation to its end or finishing a task before starting another doesn’t come from being disinterested. This happens because the brain has been wired to find stimulation in a different way.

The ADHD symptoms in adults are unnoticeable because adults have spent years developing systems, habits, and strategies to work around how much effort it actually requires to complete tasks.

The workarounds often show up as success. This increases the difficulty in identifying the symptoms. When a person has quietly restructured their life around ADHD, they may seem to be highly organized and high-achieving.

But the scaffold sometimes crashes, and the energy it took to look successful is exposed. A life event that brings changes to the home or work can bring significant damage. This is a time for seeking answers because the old system has given out.

The Symptoms That Nobody Mentions

Most know that difficulty focusing is part of ADHD. The surprise comes from newly diagnosed adults who have learned the range of symptoms that never made it onto the checklist they imagined. One of the most significant aspects is the person’s ability to maintain emotional regulation. It is the least discussed symptom of adult ADHD.

There is an intense emotional pain triggered by perceived criticism or failure called rejection-sensitive dysphoria. This can be so overwhelming that it will shape every relationship and career decision a person makes.

This dysphoria can do more damage than other focus-related symptoms. It does not take much – a facial expression, a canceled plan, a conversation that felt off. The emotional response can be swift and intense – and for most adults who experience it, the safest thing they have learned to do is act like it didn’t happen. Hiding becomes its own kind of exhaustion.

Another common ADHD symptom among adults is time blindness. This symptom shows up as an experience of time existing only in categories: now and not now. Deadlines, commitments, and appointments are abstract until they are suddenly urgent.

The flipside of this is hyperfocus. This happens when an adult locks in with extraordinary intensity on something engaging for hours. This leads to skipping meals and going without sleep. None of these symptoms is what most people see as common ADHD distracted behavior.

Hyperfocus gets mistaken for a superpower sometimes. And honestly, it can be. But it has a dark side. That same intensity can latch onto the wrong thing at the wrong time – and once it does, good luck redirecting it. The garage gets completely reorganized on a Saturday while an urgent work deadline sits untouched. The deadline doesn’t move. The brain does what it wants anyway.

ADHD Symptoms, Shame, and the Spiritual Weight They Carry

Christians with undiagnosed ADHD carry a different kind of burden. They feel as though the inability to follow through on commitments and their chronic disorganization get filtered through a moral lens instead of a neurological one.

Many of these individuals may end up internalizing the message that they are undisciplined or spiritually weak. This is a real issue that carries a real weight for some individuals. The internal critic that comes with it can be relentless. For believers, it often speaks in the language of faith.

Not every faith community knows how to hold this. The language of discipline and self-control runs deep in Christian spaces. But for someone who has spent years wondering why those things feel so far out of reach, the Sunday morning message can quietly become one more area where they feel like they’re falling short.

God’s word speaks to the mind that feels scattered and overwhelmed. In Philippians 4, the anxiousness and restless thoughts should be brought to God in prayer and trust that His peace will guard their mind. This brings hope for those who have felt like their brain has been working against them (Philippians 4:6-7). Just because it’s a neurological difference does not mean it will disqualify the adult with ADHD from receiving this peace. It just looks different.

How ADHD Symptoms in Adults Affect Relationships and Daily Life

Undiagnosed ADHD does have a relational impact that can be significant and painful. Partners of those who have ADHD symptoms feel unheard and deprioritized. At the same time, the person with ADHD feels as though they are carrying genuine love alongside a brain that loses track of details or forgets conversations.

There are times when a friendship may fade because maintaining contact requires a sustained low-stimulation effort. This can prove to be hard for an adult with ADHD.

None of it means they don’t care. The forgotten plans, the faded friendships, the conversations that slipped – that’s not indifference. That’s a brain with a full tank that somehow keeps running dry. Explaining that gap to the people who got hurt by it may be the hardest part of all.

In the workplace, these adults often feel like they are on a pendulum that swings back and forth between the alignment of the environment and the ADHD brain function. Other areas that can prove to be strenuous include financial management, long-term planning, and household organization.

In Scripture, Paul wrote about the experience of knowing what is right and the act of actually doing it. This is something that resonates deeply with many adults who grapple with this gap between intention and follow-through that ADHD has produced (Romans 7:15-20).

The gap between intention and follow-through is not a moral failing. Paul felt it. Adults with ADHD live with it. Unlike some gaps, this one can actually narrow. But it requires the right understanding and the right support behind it.

How does Christian counseling help?

Recognition alone does not resolve the years that have been spent struggling with ADHD symptoms. Professional support can be helpful with recognizing ADHD symptoms, as well as working through the relational strain and exhaustion that accompany the late diagnosis. Christian counselors are equipped to work with adults who are navigating ADHD in a way that addresses the practical challenges and the questions of identity, worth, and faith.

Good therapy for ADHD isn’t just about getting organized. It’s about dismantling a story someone has been telling themselves for decades. It is about removing the ideas that they’re lazy, that they’re not trying hard enough, and that they should just pray more. A faith-based counselor can hold the neurological and the spiritual in the same space. That combination is rarer than it should be, and it makes a real difference.

If you feel as though your life is on a pendulum between peace and anxious thoughts, your next step would be to reach out. Many Christian counselors can provide help from an informed and compassionate perspective on what ADHD symptoms look like in adults. They can also give tips on how to overcome them.

Contact our front office and speak to the reception team for more information. This will help you get started on the right pathway to understanding your brain and yourself much better.

item.title: The Benefits of Sleep: A Spiritual Discipline Worth Pursuing
item.description:
Have you ever thought at length about sleep? For several hours every day, we sleep and unplug from the world around us. We might drift into dreams, nightmares, or a restless sleep, and all the while the world carries on without us. There are many benefits of sleep, and sleep shouldn’t be something you treat as an optional extra or an inconvenience. It’s one of the Lord’s many blessings that helps us maintain our well-being.

Our Culture and Sleep

One of the things that most fitness apps and devices have is sleep monitoring. There’s a growing awareness that sleep is a significant part of a person’s health. That is often at odds with other aspects of our culture. Often, exhaustion is quietly glorified as packed schedules are seen as a sign of productivity. Admitting that you need more sleep can sometimes be read as a sign of weakness or a sign that you can’t keep up with the rest of the world.

For Christians, there’s an additional layer to all of this. Misreading the call to work diligently as unto the Lord can result in feeling like taking time to rest is self-indulgent or a failure of good stewardship. Yes, laziness is a reality, and Scripture warns us about it. For instance:

A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest – and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man. – Proverbs 24:33-34, NIV

The threat of poverty hanging over you on account of a little slumber could be enough to jolt you into constant activity, hustling daily, and staying on the grind ceaselessly. The warnings in Proverbs need to be understood in their context, as well as in the broader context of Scripture. Rest is considered a gift and a necessary part of faithful existence. The warning from Proverbs is part but not the whole of the story.

The rest of the story includes the reality of sabbath rest being woven into creation itself (Genesis 2:1-3), and taking time away from our labors was a command given to God’s people (Exodus 16; 20:8-11) patterned after God’s own ways of doing things. Even the land that people worked was supposed to be given a year of rest (Exodus 23:10-11). The Psalmist declares that:

In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for food to eat – for he grants sleep to those he loves – Psalm 127:2, NIV

Rest is not the same as laziness. More often than not, Scripture looks upon rest and sleep as a quietly defiant trust in a God who doesn’t slumber and is trustworthy. You can rest while resting assured that the One who holds it all together is keeping you safe and restoring you all at the same time.

Ways We Can Sabotage Our Sleep

There are some bad habits and unhelpful ideas regarding sleep that can end up sabotaging it. It’s helpful to identify the misconceptions or myths about sleep that can keep you stuck or make it harder for you to get your rest. Getting your mindset right about sleep will better position you to take hold of its benefits.

One mistake we can make is to minimize the role sleep plays in our lives. The seven to nine hours that sleep takes up each day are not dead space or unproductive time. Far from being a passive thing, sleep is one of the most metabolically active periods of the day. While you sleep, your body is doing some important work, including your brain consolidating memories, clearing out cellular waste products, and repairing tissue.

Another myth is the idea that you can stay busy during the week, and you can simply catch up on your sleep over the weekend. When you have a chronic sleep debt, that’s not something you can remedy in just two days. Sleeping in over the weekend certainly helps, but there is a physiological and cognitive cost to disrupted sleep. That cost accumulates in ways that a few extra hours of sleep can’t remedy. You need consistent sleep for that to happen.

You might also sabotage your sleep by not giving yourself adequate time for it. Not only is it important to get downtime before you actually sleep, but you then need to have enough hours of sleep each night. Some people can function well on less sleep, but that’s not most of us.

Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep so that they don’t wake up feeling groggy and can function at their best. Poor sleep hygiene can often result in getting irritable more quickly and not thinking clearly.

Simply getting to sleep on time can be a huge challenge. Whether it’s procrastination, getting caught up watching your favorite series, attending to your children or your chores, doomscrolling, or simply being restless thinking about the next day, it can be difficult to get to bed on time. If you don’t allow yourself enough downtime before bed, falling asleep with enough time to give you a full night’s rest might not happen.

The Benefits of Sleep

What does sleep actually do for you? One of the major ways you can motivate yourself to make changes that will help your sleep is to understand what the benefits of great sleep are. The changes that you may need to make can seem inconvenient, but the benefits you reap from good sleep make it more than worth it.

Some of the main benefits of sleep include:

Emotional regulation When you don’t sleep well, you may find yourself struggling to regulate your emotions as effectively as you do when you’re well rested. When you’ve slept well, you’re better able to respond patiently to conflict, you can manage your frustrations a bit easier, and you can face difficulty more optimistically.

Sleep helps a person address concerns such as irritability, a persistent low mood, or emotional reactivity. When you’re sleeping well, you’re in a much better position to face these challenges. You may notice that you are more patient, quick to listen, and slow to anger.

Physical well-being When you’re sleep-deprived, you’re at an increased risk for depression, anxiety, weight gain, and several chronic health conditions. Getting good sleep isn’t a cure-all for ailments, but it supports hormonal balance, better immune function, cardiovascular health, and your body’s ability to manage inflammation.

Spiritual wellness There are so many things to be anxious about as we go about our lives. We worry about work, our children, the state of our world, our health, and so much else. Going to sleep can be seen and practiced as a discipline. Hustle culture says that going to sleep can seem like a waste of time, but it can be a counter-cultural form of trust when we choose rest over productivity.

Going to sleep when it feels like the world is falling apart can be a huge step of faith. Not only is resting a good idea to help us gain perspective on things, but it can rightly be seen as an embodied acknowledgment that the Lord is God and we are not. The world doesn’t depend on our constant activity or vigilance. Rather, the Lord is the one who sustains all things, and He does not sleep (Psalms 121:1-8; Hebrews 1:3).

Getting a full night’s rest consistently can help to promote your well-being, emotionally, physically, and spiritually. What seems like a pointless surrender to inactivity for a few hours out of every day is actually one of the Lord’s greatest gifts to us. His invitation for us to rest, not only spiritually by resting in His perfect work through Jesus, but also physically by ceasing our labors, can help restore much-needed balance and wellness.

Next Steps to Get Great Sleep

When you want to make changes that last, the way to do that isn’t necessarily by making huge and dramatic overhauls. Making small but impactful changes and then sticking to them can make all the difference. Some places where you can start include the following:

Set a wake time Being consistent in when you wake up can make a significant difference in regulating your body’s clock. Choose a time when you’ll wake up and then stick to that for a couple of weeks before you move on to adjust other things.

Have a wind-down ritual For example, a forty-five-minute wind-down ritual can help if you find it hard to settle your mind before bed. This time is to allow your brain the time it needs to transition from the day’s activities toward the quiet of sleep. Your ritual could include dimming lights, stretching, praying and reading Scripture, or listening to gentle music. It’s best to put down your screens at this time.

Make your bedroom a place for sleep Your bedroom isn’t a multipurpose room, so if possible, avoid working or watching emotionally intense content there. The point is to create the association between your bedroom and rest, so when you’re in the room, you start to transition toward sleep much more easily.

Limit caffeine An afternoon coffee can still be active in your system around bedtime, so it’s important to cut yourself off about five to six hours before bedtime. Limiting energy drinks can also help your sleep.

Getting good sleep benefits you in many ways. Sleep can rightly be seen as a spiritual discipline, a way to surrender ourselves to God in a tangible way that also promotes our well-being. Struggling to sleep can be a symptom of depression, anxiety, or grief. If you find yourself experiencing sleep difficulties despite having good sleep habits, speak with a doctor or a counselor.

If you’re struggling with getting good sleep, you can reach out to our office to connect with a Christian counselor in Alamo Ranch, Texas, who can help you process some potential causes of sleeplessness.

item.title: What Many People Misunderstand About Borderline Personality Disorder
item.description:
If you have ever had an exposed nerve ending in your tooth, you will know how painful and miserable an experience that can be. Although you could not see the issue, you would have been aware of it every time you chewed food on the side of your mouth where the nerve was exposed. Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is like having multiple exposed nerves that cause overwhelming emotional pain most of the time.

Simple events can feel devastating. You live with a constant feeling that your loved ones are going to leave you, and you often experience overwhelming mood shifts. Your nervous system is in deep distress, and there is no equivalent of a dental filling to protect your emotions from the pain.

When you live your life as an impulsive, reactive, deeply emotional person, your relationships cannot help but be affected. Not only are relationships more complicated with Borderline Personality Disorder, but you frequently experience the one thing you fear the most: people leaving you.

Some people simply do not have the capacity or the compassion to stick by you. Other times, you push people away because of how BPD affects your view of others. You either see people as shining examples of everything right with humanity or as the devil incarnate, incapable of being good.

Borderline personality disorder is a mental health condition defined by black-and-white thinking, this or that, with no in between. It is exhausting to live experiencing such extremes, and most people with BPD are internally exhausted from having to experience everything they do. However, it is possible to recover from BPD, to learn to have emotionally stable relationships and friendships, and to be emotionally regulated. It is a long journey that begins with understanding yourself.

The Diagnostic Criteria for Borderline Personality Disorder

People who suspect they have BPD generally display the following symptoms for years: a history of instability in relationships, regular, extreme angry outbursts, impulsive behavior with disruptive consequences, and frequent, intense mood shifts. Behavioral traits like these might be attached to several trauma-related experiences, like PTSD or CPTSD. A mental health expert can confirm an official diagnosis of BPD if five of the following nine symptoms are ongoing and disruptive to your life.

(Note that this is not a tool to self-diagnose, or to diagnose someone else, but it is simply the diagnostic criteria that psychiatrists use to determine Borderline Personality Disorder.)

Frantic Attempts to Avoid Abandonment

With BPD, it constantly feels like people are preparing to cut you loose from their lives. Things as simple as an unanswered text message or a perceived change in mood cause you to spiral and to do whatever you can to avoid the seemingly inevitable abandonment. This could mean even threatening suicidal behavior as a way of getting their attention and keeping them from leaving you.

Unstable and Intense Relationships

People with Borderline personality disorder can only see others through a black-and-white lens, with no neutral shades. This means they see others as entirely good or entirely bad, with no blending of traits.

As if this were not unhealthy enough, there might be a random moment when their view of someone suddenly flips. They go from having that person placed on a pedestal to villainizing their every action. This makes for turbulent relationships and connections with others, ironically ensuring that others abandon them, just as they anticipated.

Identity Disturbances

Just as they see others in terms of black-and-white judgments, their sense of self-worth is similarly extreme. They tend to either feel like the most important person in the room or the most worthless, with the tendency to flip from one to the other with little warning. Along with rapid shifts in their self-esteem, their preferences, interests, and values continually change too.

Chronic Impulsivity

People with BPD have frequent, disruptive, impulsive behavior, which causes a variety of issues. From excessive spending to making major life choices on a whim to engaging in harmful behavior with others, this impulsive behavior is as destructive as it is unpredictable. The issue with chronic impulsivity like this is that there are often long-term consequences, and some of them are difficult to walk back.

Extreme Mood Swings and Instability

A person with BPD can go from a state of euphoria to anger and to anxiety over the space of a week. They experience each mood intensely for up to two days before moving on to the next mood. Of course, none of it is intentional, and they often know that none of the emotions are rational while feeling them. However, trying to regulate such intense emotions is like trying to calm a tsunami wave.

Chronic Feelings of Emptiness

After several dramatic mood swings, a person with Borderline personality disorder usually comes back to a baseline of feeling lonely, bored, and empty. Loneliness and emptiness are sometimes so intense that they become suicidal or resort to self-harm to feel something different. Some people with BPD describe their most stable, constant moods as being lonely or numb.

Extreme Anger That Is Hard to Control

Anger is often a logical response to injustice or unfairness. However, for the person with BPD, anger is most often disconnected from current events or is a disproportionate response. It frequently leads to physical aggression and threats, often with dire consequences.

Feeling Disconnected From Reality

When not feeling irrationally angry, empty, or on an emotional roller coaster, people with BPD tend to dissociate from reality. They might feel an out-of-body experience, or as if nothing around them is real. This mood does not persist for long, but it is unnerving each time it happens.

Repeated Crisis Behaviors Under Stress

More than most people, those with Borderline personality disorder engage in self-harm and suicidality when under stress. This behavior ranges from threats to suicide attempts, and overdoses on medication. It is often because they feel overwhelmed by the feeling of loneliness that they resort to these actions.

Recovery and Hope for a Future

All is not lost for those with Borderline Personality Disorder. Many people who spent decades struggling with the disorder eventually improved to the point of no longer meeting diagnostic criteria. It is not an easy or fast road, but with a combination of the right medication, therapy, and determination, it is possible that you can make as full a recovery as you could hope for.

It is helpful to know some terminology that is part of the recovery journey with BPD, however. If you have incorporated counseling or therapy as a regular part of your mental wellness, you might experience symptomatic remission. This is when you have become stable and no longer meet the diagnostic criteria for Borderline Personality Disorder.

This is an achievement to celebrate, because it means that you have conquered much already. At this stage, it is advisable that you still receive counseling and support for your mental health, as some people experience relapses even when they thought they had recovered.

Recovery comes several years after symptomatic remission. When you have been asymptomatic for years, when you have managed to participate in several balanced, long-term relationships, and have had no disruptions from unruly emotions, you can finally say that you have recovered. The point is that recovery is possible and that it is worth the effort, focus, and perseverance it takes to achieve.

It can often feel like you are too damaged to heal, or that too much has happened ever to be able to experience stability and calm. Both feelings are valid, but the truth is far more optimistic. You can have a life without exhausting emotional swings; you can have relationships without excessive drama, and you can find love without fear of losing it. You just need to ask yourself if you are willing to risk the journey to find it.

Borderline Personality Disorder is not easy to deal with alone. We host an online catalog of counselors where we hope you will find someone to walk with you. Alternatively, our reception team can help you find a counselor according to your specifications and preferences.
